claims.text: Active-learning neural-network potentials can drastically reduce the cost of computing fusion and high-temperature free energies.
The proposed method can preserve fidelity to anharmonic, vibrational, and electron–vibration effects.
The initial target domain is elemental and binary metallic systems near their melting points.
The intervention trains a neural-network interatomic potential on a sparse set of ab initio configurations.
Targeted active-learning iterations refine the potential using configurations from both solid and liquid phase space.
The proposed operating temperature range extends from just below melting to approximately 1.5 times the melting temperature.
A neural-network potential can represent detailed configurational energetics, including anharmonic vibrational modes and entropy contributions.
Accurate representation of configurational energetics mediates the accuracy of predicted free energies.
Active sampling of critical phase-space regions allows the potential to capture the complex free-energy landscape with fewer ab initio calculations.
Iterative refinement captures vibrational entropy and anharmonicity while maintaining fidelity relative to explicit molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations.
The proposed method will achieve free-energy errors within a few meV per atom.
The proposed method will provide a computational speedup of approximately one to two orders of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method will scale better than TOR-TILD.
The predicted performance remains valid up to 1.5 times the melting point when electronic and vibrational coupling does not deviate extremely from metallic behavior.
Extreme anharmonicity or non-metallic bonding may degrade the method's performance.
Transferability to highly multicomponent high-entropy alloys and systems with strongly nonlinear electron–vibration coupling is uncertain.
